content: Preeclampsia is a significant cause of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide. It is characterized by the onset of hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation or near term, accompanied by proteinuria or other signs of maternal organ dysfunction. Proteinuria may not always be present, in which case other maternal organ dysfunctions should be evaluated. The previous classification of preeclampsia into mild and severe is no longer used because the condition can worsen suddenly at any stage. Pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastric region may result from periportal and focal parenchymal liver necrosis, hepatic cell edema, or distension of Glisson’s capsule. However, liver pathology does not always correlate with laboratory findings. Headache is not a reliable symptom of severe preeclampsia, and other neurological abnormalities should be assessed. Symptoms such as headache, blurred vision, scotoma, hyperreflexia, temporary blindness, or tonic-clonic seizures may occur. The occurrence of tonic-clonic seizures defines eclampsia. Eclampsia was first identified by François Mauriceau, a French obstetrician born in 1637, who noted a correlation between convulsions in primigravidas and suppressed lochial flow or intrauterine fetal death. Preeclampsia may result from placental factors entering the maternal circulation, leading to endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, and proteinuria. Elevated levels of an anti-angiogenic factor, fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), in the placenta are associated with endothelial dysfunction. Apoptosis in the villous trophoblast of preeclamptic women has also been observed. Uteroplacental ischemia and incomplete invasion of spiral arteries by trophoblasts can release angiogenic factors, causing systemic organ involvement. Genetic factors, including incomplete gene penetration, may also contribute to the pathogenesis of preeclampsia. Common causes of preeclampsia include uteroplacental ischemia, genetic predisposition, oxidative stress in trophoblast cells, apoptosis in trophoblast cells, systemic inflammatory responses, vasospasm, platelet aggregation, thrombin formation, and fibrin deposition in multiple organs. Preeclampsia is classified based on the timing of onset into early preeclampsia (before 34 weeks of gestation) and late preeclampsia (after delivery). It is no longer diagnosed solely based on proteinuria due to the high rate of false negatives. Instead, diagnostic criteria include blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg, evidence of maternal organ involvement, and other clinical features. The prevalence of preeclampsia is approximately 2,000–8,000 cases per 100,000 pregnancies worldwide. In the United States, the incidence was estimated at 25,000 cases per 100,000 pregnancies between 1987 and 2004. Preeclampsia is more common in women younger than 20 or older than 40 years and is frequently observed in non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, and American Indian/Alaska Native populations. Risk factors for preeclampsia include nulliparity, multifetal gestations, a history of preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy, chronic hypertension, pregestational or gestational diabetes, thrombophilia, systemic lupus erythematosus, a body mass index greater than 30 at the start of prenatal care, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, maternal age ≥35 years, kidney disease, assisted reproductive technology, obstructive sleep apnea, and African-American descent. Routine screening for preeclampsia is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. Early clinical features after 20 weeks of gestation include elevated blood pressure (≥140/90 mmHg), proteinuria, and evidence of maternal organ involvement. Common complications include intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), uteroplacental insufficiency, fetal asphyxia or death, maternal seizures, and maternal death. Long-term complications include chronic hypertension, diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, kidney disease, thromboembolism, hypothyroidism, and impaired memory. Preeclampsia may present for the first time during labor or in the early postpartum period. All hypertensive pregnant women should be evaluated for symptoms of organ damage, even in the absence of proteinuria. Symptoms of preeclampsia may include epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, frontal or occipital headache, visual scotoma, shortness of breath, limb swelling, altered mental status, and photophobia. Physical examination findings in preeclampsia often include edema. Additional findings may include hyperreflexia, vision loss or deficits, altered sensorium, confusion, rales in the lungs, and limb edema. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) should be considered in patients with vision loss, seizures, headache, or altered mental status. Laboratory findings consistent with preeclampsia include elevated liver enzymes, thrombocytopenia, elevated serum creatinine, and elevated serum uric acid. HELLP syndrome is diagnosed by elevated liver enzymes, low platelets, and hemolysis. There are no specific ultrasound findings associated with preeclampsia, but ultrasound may be useful for monitoring fetal complications such as growth restriction. Similarly, there are no specific MRI findings for preeclampsia, but brain MRI may help diagnose complications such as PRES, which is characterized by vasogenic edema and hyperintensities in the posterior brain regions. The goal of therapy is to initiate treatment for blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg in clinical settings or ≥135/85 mmHg at home, aiming for a target systolic blood pressure of 110–140 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure <85 mmHg. First-line antihypertensive medications include oral methyldopa, labetalol, oxprenolol, and nifedipine. Secondor third-line agents include hydralazine and prazosin. Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) is the treatment of choice for seizure prophylaxis in patients with proteinuria and severe hypertension or hypertension with neurological symptoms. Urgent therapy for severe hypertension (blood pressure >160/110 mmHg) includes oral nifedipine, intravenous labetalol, hydralazine, or oral labetalol. Delivery is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia and is recommended at 37 weeks of gestation or earlier if severe complications occur, such as repeated episodes of severe hypertension, progressive thrombocytopenia, worsening renal or liver function, pulmonary edema, neurological abnormalities, stroke, myocardial infarction, HELLP syndrome, eclampsia, suspected placental abruption, abnormal fetal testing, fetal death, or a fetus with no expectation of survival. Secondary prevention strategies after preeclampsia include blood pressure monitoring, repeated proteinuria assessments if initial results are negative, clinical evaluation for clonus, and twice-weekly blood tests to monitor hemoglobin, platelet count, uric acid, liver enzymes, and renal function.
